title: ChatGPT Gets a Wallet
summary: OpenAI's new ChatGPT Wallet lets the assistant's agents buy things for you, charging a payment token instead of your card number — while Amazon and other retailers move to block the door.
content:
On Friday, OpenAI turned ChatGPT from a thing that talks about shopping into a thing that shops. The new ChatGPT Wallet lets the assistant's agents — OpenAI calls them "dots" — pick items, fill a cart, and complete the checkout on your behalf. It is the most concrete step yet from a major lab toward AI that spends money, not just suggests where to spend it.

What shipped

The feature is live for a limited set of US ChatGPT Pro subscribers, 18 and up, holding a US-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express. You add an eligible card once, then ask your dot to handle a purchase. When it is time to pay, you review the item, the total, and the card that will be charged, and you approve the transaction with a biometric check like Face ID or a fingerprint. That approval also writes a record of the purchase.

OpenAI is explicit that the human stays in the loop at launch. The limited rollout is framed as a test before a wider release, and the company says future versions will add spending limits and rules around categories or time windows, so you can pre-approve purchases and let the agent act with less supervision.

The token trick

The interesting part is plumbing, not shopping. ChatGPT does not hand your card number to the dot or the merchant. Instead it charges the selected card using a payment token — a stand-in that maps back to your account without exposing the underlying details. Merchants still get what they need to ship the order, like the address and contact info, supplied by the dot.

Crucially, you keep the card's normal protections: rewards still accrue, and you can still dispute a charge. That matters, because the pitch only works if agentic payments feel like an extension of the card you already trust rather than a new financial relationship with a chatbot.

The retailer counter-move

The friction is not technical. It is commercial. Amazon — the largest online retailer in the US — blocks AI agents from shopping its site, steering customers toward its own assistant, Alexa. Other retailers have followed with similar walls, worried about ceding the checkout to someone else's agent. To push back, OpenAI published a Commerce Partner Playbook with tools and guidance for sites that want to support agent-driven buyers.

That standoff is the real story. Agentic commerce only scales if merchants agree to be bought from by software they do not control, and many would rather keep the customer relationship — and the upsell — for themselves. Whoever wins that negotiation decides how much of retail runs through a chat window.

Why now

The timing is not arbitrary. DoorDash and Uber report low volumes of agent-placed orders, but Meta's Muse, past 10 million users, has found AI-assisted shopping to be one of its top activities. Smaller players like Instinct already buy on users' behalf. OpenAI is entering a market where demand is showing up before the infrastructure is settled.

Takeaway

ChatGPT Wallet is less a product than a land grab: OpenAI wants to own the moment of purchase, and it is starting with the one thing that makes that safe — a token that keeps your card number out of the loop. The tech is ready. The question is whether retailers will let an agent they do not own walk through their checkout, or keep building walls. Watch Amazon's stance, and watch whether OpenAI's spending controls arrive before the open beta does. The wallet is open; the fight over who gets to use it has just started.
